Comparing `predicted == y_true` element-wise checks for exact numeric agreement, which fails completely under this swap even though the underlying grouping is identical, producing a misleadingly terrible-looking 0.0. `adjusted_rand_score` (and similar clustering metrics) evaluate whether two groupings agree on *which points are grouped together*, regardless of which arbitrary integer label got attached to each group, which is the only comparison that actually makes sense for unsupervised output -- a direct reminder that unsupervised results have no inherent mapping to any external label space.

model.fit(X)
predicted = model.labels_

score = adjusted_rand_score(y_true, predicted)
print(score)  # 1.0 -- the grouping is actually perfect

Notice the negative error at index 1 and index 3 contributed positively to the sum once squared, exactly why squaring is used -- a raw, unsquared average would have partially canceled positive and negative errors against each other and understated how wrong the predictions actually were.

In the original code, `y_pred` is computed exactly once, before the loop starts, using w=0.0. Even though `w` is updated on every iteration afterward, nothing ever recomputes `y_pred` from that new value -- `loss = mse(y, y_pred)` keeps reading the exact same stale `y_pred` list every time, so the printed loss is bitwise identical on every step despite `w` visibly changing. The fix moves the `y_pred = [...]` line inside the loop, after `w` is updated, so predictions -- and therefore the loss computed from them -- genuinely reflect the current parameter value on every single iteration. This is a very real bug pattern: updating a parameter but not recomputing everything downstream of it that a later calculation depends on.
